originalGroup.material:
A. Your first newspaper interview

You have joined the school newspaper and are about to interview someone for the first time. You may feel that a good reporter must always know what to say. In fact, some preparation and careful listening matter more than a loud, confident voice.

Before arranging the interview, decide what you want readers to learn. A conversation about winning a race will be different from one about starting a new club. ____1____ This focus will help you choose a few useful questions instead of preparing a long list of unrelated ones.

Send the person a short message explaining your topic and asking for a suitable time. ____2____ A ten-minute conversation during a quiet break may be more useful than stopping someone who is already late for class.

During the interview, listen to the whole answer. Do not spend every moment looking for the next question on your page. ____3____ For example, if a player mentions a difficult decision, you could ask what made it difficult. Such a follow-up grows naturally from the answer.

Make notes, but check any detail you are uncertain about. ____4____ It is better to ask someone to repeat a name than to print the wrong one. If you want to record the conversation, get permission first.

Finally, explain when the article is likely to appear and thank the person. ____5____ Your written questions may have started the interview, but another person's time and experience made the story possible.

B. A shadow on the wall

Hill School's science club ____1____ (found) in 2019. Last month its members visited the ____2____ (old) building on the school grounds; none of the other buildings was as old. After ____3____ (visit) the small exhibition inside, they noticed ____4____ unusual metal shape above the door. A teacher explained that it was part of a sundial, an instrument ____5____ shows the time by the position of a shadow.

Back in their classroom, the students looked ____6____ (careful) at photographs of the wall. They decided ____7____ (share) what they had learned with younger ____8____ (child) at the school. Working in pairs, they made simple paper models and placed them beside a sunny window. They soon discovered that moving a model changed its reading, so they marked one position on the table and left each model there.

On the exhibition day, the club not only displayed the models ____9____ also invited visitors to watch the shadows move. The visitors asked many questions. When the event ended, the club kept the models and stored ____10____ (they) in a cupboard for the next science lesson. The old object above the door had given the students a new way to notice the passing of an ordinary afternoon.

originalGroup.material:
A. Notes that remain useful

Opening a notebook a week after a lesson can be a surprising experience. A page that seemed perfectly clear at the time may now look like a list of disconnected words. Useful notes need to help the person you will be later, when the teacher's explanation is no longer in your ears.

Start by giving each page a clear topic and date. ____1____ Without those small signs, even accurate details may be difficult to place when you return to the notebook before an exam.

During the lesson, do not try to copy every sentence. Listen for the relationship between ideas. ____2____ For instance, an arrow labelled 'because' records something that two isolated facts cannot show. Use a symbol only if you will still understand it next week.

Leave room beside a point that you have not understood. Some students are tempted to fill every space so that the page looks complete. ____3____ A visible question tells you what to ask about; a confident-looking line copied without understanding does not.

Soon after the lesson, close the book and try to explain its main idea aloud. Then check your account against the page. ____4____ Add a short explanation at that point, while the lesson is still fresh enough to recall.

Finally, let the notebook change as your understanding develops. You may find a better example in a later lesson or discover that two topics are connected. ____5____ The aim is a record you can think with, not a page that remains exactly as it looked on the day it was written.

B. Behind the paper screen

For the past three weeks, our drama group ____1____ (prepare) a shadow play, and today we are ready to perform it. The story is about a traveller ____2____ loses a map but finds help in an unfamiliar village. Instead of using a large stage, we are working behind ____3____ white paper screen.

At first, we cut the figures from thin paper. They bent so ____4____ (easy) that their shapes were difficult to control. Our teacher suggested ____5____ (use) thicker card. That solved one problem, but the heavier figures needed stronger handles. After several attempts, we found a way to attach wooden sticks to ____6____ (they) without covering any important part of the picture.

Yesterday, our final practice ____7____ (interrupt) by a power cut. We could not use the lamp, so we sat beside the window and read our lines aloud. The unexpected pause helped us notice that the traveller's last speech was much ____8____ (long) than the others. We shortened it before leaving.

Now the light is working again. We are not certain ____9____ the audience will enjoy every scene, but we know the story clearly. As we take our places, our teacher reminds us that the figures must stay close ____10____ the screen if we want their shadows to have clear edges.
